reason: The citation is right and the line is still wrong to ship bare. The 1825 scan was downloaded whole and read: the title page prints THE WORKS OF ANNA LAETITIA BARBAULD, WITH A MEMOIR BY LUCY AIKIN, IN TWO VOLUMES, VOL. I, PRINTED FOR LONGMAN, HURST, REES, ORME, BROWN, AND GREEN, 1825; the contents give The Rights of Woman 185; p. 185 heads the poem and line 1 reads YES, injured Woman! rise, assert thy right! So wording, page, volume, editor and imprint all check out, the opening capitals are typographic, and shipped.js gives anna laetitia barbauld 0 of 3, not banned, nothing shipped, no near opening. What breaks it is the poem, which I read to the end on the same scan. It is a palinode: it runs through Thy rights are empire: urge no meaner claim, and Make treacherous Man thy subject, not thy friend; / Thou mayst command, but never canst be free, and closes on p. 187 with Then, then, abandon each ambitious thought, / Conquest or rule thy heart shall feebly move, / In Nature's school, by her soft maxims taught, / That separate rights are lost in mutual love. The first line is the position the poem exists to retract, and the reading that Barbauld wrote it against Wollstonecraft, who had attacked her in the Vindication, is the standard one (reported from memory, the web search budget being spent). This is precisely the case the brief's own misattribution sheet legislates for: real, famous, and nearly always misread, where the note must carry the gloss, as it requires for Sartre's Hell is other people and Frost's ironic reading. The note here is empty, and the month already carries two Wollstonecraft lines, so as it stands September would print Barbauld as seconding a poem she wrote to answer. Refuted as presented. It can be rescued only one way: keep the citation exactly as it is and add a note saying plainly that the poem turns against its own opening and ends that separate rights are lost in mutual love, so the reader is not sold the first line as Barbauld's settled position. If the editor will not carry that note, drop the line; the September slot is better filled by Lanyer or Wilcox, whose poems mean at the end what they say at the start.
